title: Why Is Working Memory So Important for Learning
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Carl Hendrick makes the case that working memory, despite its modest capacity, exerts an outsized influence on all learning and should shape how teachers design instruction. He traces the idea from George Miller's 'magic number' seven, through later research suggesting a limit closer to four chunks, to Baddeley and Hitch's model of working memory as an active workspace rather than a passive store. He stresses that working memory is highly vulnerable to disruption by distraction, stress and environment, and that Baddeley's central executive ties it to attentional control. From there he links working memory limits to the critique of minimally guided discovery learning and to Cognitive Load Theory's distinction between intrinsic and extraneous load. The move of the piece is to turn a theoretical construct into a practical imperative: modelling, guided practice, scaffolding and removing distractions all serve the single purpose of protecting working memory.
points: Hendrick frames working memory as an active workspace for holding and manipulating information, following Baddeley and Hitch, rather than the passive short-term store of older models, with capacity closer to four meaningful chunks than Miller's seven.
Because working memory is so easily disrupted by distraction, emotional state or environment, he argues that phones are especially damaging to deep learning.

Effective instruction is about supporting attention as well as reducing load: clear routines, minimal distractions and predictable structure preserve the attentional control working memory depends on.

He locates the core objection to discovery learning in working memory overload when learners lack knowledge in long-term memory, and boils Cognitive Load Theory down to designing instruction to manage intrinsic and extraneous load.
Modelling, guided practice, scaffolding and removing distractions are presented as one family of techniques whose shared purpose is protecting working memory.
quotes: The strange thing about working memory is that despite its modest capacity, it exerts an outsized influence on all learning outcomes. It’s also one of those things that most people think they know how it works but it’s only relatively recently that we’ve understood the limits of our understanding.

This idea laid the groundwork for understanding cognitive capacity, but later research refined it further, suggesting that working memory is even more limited, closer to four meaningful chunks. Crucially, it’s not just a passive store, but an active workspace where information is held, processed, and manipulated in real time.

Unlike long-term memory which can store vast amounts of information for decades, working memory is remarkably vulnerable to disruption. A simple distraction, emotional state, or even classroom environmental factors can dramatically reduce its already limited capacity, which is why phones are so disastrous for deep learning.

Effective instruction, then, isn’t just about reducing load, it’s about supporting attention. Clear routines, minimal distractions, and predictable structure help preserve the limited attentional control that working memory depends on.

Understanding the limits of WM is really key to creating effective learning environments. If I had to boil down CLT to one thing, it would be that instruction must be designed to manage these loads, or learning won't happen.

This is why techniques like modelling, guided practice, scaffolding, and removing distractions all serve one purpose: they protect working memory. They help students devote their limited resources to the actual content, rather than wasting it processing irrelevant information.
